FROST Explained: Schnorr Threshold Signatures for Bitcoin

Alexander Nemish — Feb 5, 2026

Contents

  • Introduction
  • Schnorr Signatures — elliptic curve setup, signing, verification, and why nonces matter
  • Aggregating Nonce R — binding factors and why naive aggregation is dangerous
  • Aggregating Partial Signatures — share equations, sum correctness, identifiable abort
  • Shamir Secret Sharing — polynomials, Pedersen DKG, Feldman VSS

Introduction

Imagine a Bitcoin wallet controlled by a company with five board members. You want a rule: any three of the five can authorize a transaction, but no one or two members can steal the funds. And when the transaction hits the blockchain, it should look exactly like any other — nobody can tell it was signed by a group.

This is exactly what FROST does. FROST stands for Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures. It lets ttt out of nnn participants jointly produce a Schnorr signature — without any single party ever knowing the full secret key. The output is a standard Schnorr signature, indistinguishable from one created by a single signer.

This is directly relevant to Bitcoin. Since the Taproot upgrade (2021), Bitcoin natively supports Schnorr signatures (BIP-340) for transaction authorization. FROST produces standard Schnorr signatures on the secp256k1 curve — exactly what Bitcoin expects. This makes FROST a natural fit for threshold signing of Bitcoin transactions: custody solutions, cross-chain bridges, or any setup where multiple parties must approve a spend, without revealing on-chain that a threshold scheme was used at all.

Why not just use a regular private key? Because a single key is a single point of failure. Stolen key — all funds gone. Lost key — all funds locked forever. FROST distributes trust: no single participant can sign alone, and any ttt of the nnn participants can cooperate to sign. The rest can be offline, unreachable, or even compromised — as long as fewer than ttt are malicious, the key is safe.

To understand how FROST achieves this, we'll build up from its foundations, one step at a time:

  1. Schnorr signatures — the signature scheme FROST is built on
  2. Nonce aggregation — how multiple signers combine their randomness into one
  3. Partial signature aggregation — how individual contributions sum to a valid signature
  4. Shamir secret sharing — how to split a secret so that any ttt of nnn pieces can reconstruct it
  5. Lagrange interpolation — the mathematical tool that makes reconstruction work
  6. The FROST protocol — putting it all together

Throughout the article, we'll use concrete numeric examples you can verify by hand. In real cryptography, all numbers are 256-bit integers and the math happens on elliptic curves, but the logic is identical.

Schnorr Signatures

Before we can distribute a signature across multiple parties, we need to understand how a single-signer Schnorr signature works.

The setup: elliptic curve math in 30 seconds

All the math happens in a cyclic group — think of it as a set of points on an elliptic curve. The group has a generator point GGG and a prime order qqq (the total number of points). We have one operation: scalar multiplication — multiplying GGG by an integer sss to get a new point s⋅Gs \cdot Gs⋅G.

The critical property: given sss and GGG, computing s⋅Gs \cdot Gs⋅G is trivial (milliseconds on a laptop). But given s⋅Gs \cdot Gs⋅G and GGG, recovering sss is computationally infeasible — this is the discrete logarithm problem, and it's the foundation of elliptic curve cryptography.

Think of it like mixing paint: combining yellow and blue to get green is easy, but looking at the green and figuring out the exact ratio of yellow and blue is practically impossible.

With that in mind, a signer has:

  • Secret key: a random number sss (a "scalar" — just a big integer modulo qqq)
  • Public key: Y=s⋅GY = s \cdot GY=s⋅G (a point on the curve — easy to compute from sss, impossible to reverse)

How signing works

To sign a message mmm, the signer:

  1. Picks a random nonce kkk and computes the commitment R=k⋅GR = k \cdot GR=k⋅G. The nonce is a one-time secret random number. "Commitment" because RRR publicly commits the signer to their choice of kkk without revealing kkk itself (discrete log again).

  2. Computes the challenge c=H(R∥Y∥m)c = H(R \| Y \| m)c=H(R∥Y∥m). This hashes together the commitment, the public key, and the message. The hash acts as an unpredictable "question" that the signer must answer — and crucially, it depends on RRR, so the signer can't know ccc before committing to their nonce. We'll see why this matters right after verification.

  3. Computes the response z=k+s⋅cz = k + s \cdot cz=k+s⋅c. This is the core equation — it blends the nonce with the secret key, weighted by the challenge. It's the "answer" to the challenge that proves the signer knows sss.

  4. Outputs the signature σ=(R,z)\sigma = (R, z)σ=(R,z) — the commitment point and the response scalar.

How verification works

Anyone with the public key YYY can verify the signature by checking:

z⋅G=?R+c⋅Yz \cdot G \stackrel{?}{=} R + c \cdot Yz⋅G=?R+c⋅Y

This reads: "multiply the generator by the response zzz, and check if it equals the commitment RRR plus the challenge times the public key."

Why does this equation hold? Let's expand the right side by substituting what RRR and YYY actually are:

R+c⋅Y=k⋅G+c⋅(s⋅G)=(k+s⋅c)⋅G=z⋅G✓R + c \cdot Y = k \cdot G + c \cdot (s \cdot G) = (k + s \cdot c) \cdot G = z \cdot G \quad \checkmarkR+c⋅Y=k⋅G+c⋅(s⋅G)=(k+s⋅c)⋅G=z⋅G✓

The equation works because we defined z=k+s⋅cz = k + s \cdot cz=k+s⋅c. A verifier who doesn't know kkk or sss can still check this — they only need the public values RRR, YYY, ccc, and zzz.

Why RRR must be in the challenge hash

Now that we've seen how verification works, we can understand why the challenge c=H(R∥Y∥m)c = H(R \| Y \| m)c=H(R∥Y∥m) must include RRR. Without it, the scheme is completely broken — anyone can forge signatures without knowing the secret key.

Suppose the challenge were just c=H(Y∥m)c = H(Y \| m)c=H(Y∥m) — no RRR. An attacker wants to forge a signature on message mmm under public key YYY:

  1. Compute c=H(Y∥m)c = H(Y \| m)c=H(Y∥m) — this is public knowledge, no secrets needed.
  2. Pick any random zzz.
  3. Compute R=z⋅G−c⋅YR = z \cdot G - c \cdot YR=z⋅G−c⋅Y.
  4. Output (R,z)(R, z)(R,z) as the "signature."

Does it verify? z⋅G=?R+c⋅Y=(z⋅G−c⋅Y)+c⋅Y=z⋅Gz \cdot G \stackrel{?}{=} R + c \cdot Y = (z \cdot G - c \cdot Y) + c \cdot Y = z \cdot Gz⋅G=?R+c⋅Y=(z⋅G−c⋅Y)+c⋅Y=z⋅G. Yes — a complete forgery without knowing the secret key.

The attack works because the forger gets to choose zzz and RRR simultaneously, engineering them to satisfy the verification equation. By including RRR in the hash, we force the signer to commit to RRR before the challenge ccc is determined. A forger would need to find RRR such that c=H(R∥Y∥m)c = H(R \| Y \| m)c=H(R∥Y∥m) and z⋅G=R+c⋅Yz \cdot G = R + c \cdot Yz⋅G=R+c⋅Y hold simultaneously — but they can't know ccc until they fix RRR, and they can't construct RRR without knowing ccc. This circular dependency is what makes forgery infeasible.

This construction is called the Fiat-Shamir transform (Fiat & Shamir, CRYPTO 1986): it converts an interactive identification protocol into a non-interactive signature scheme by replacing the verifier's random challenge with a hash of the commitment. Pointcheval & Stern (EUROCRYPT 1996) proved that this construction is existentially unforgeable in the random oracle model.

Why YYY must be in the challenge hash

Including RRR prevents forgery, but why is the public key YYY also in the hash? Without it, signatures aren't bound to a specific key — an attacker can take someone else's valid signature and claim it was signed by a different key.

Suppose the challenge were c=H(R∥m)c = H(R \| m)c=H(R∥m) — no YYY. Given a valid signature (R,z)(R, z)(R,z) for message mmm under public key YYY, an attacker can find a different public key Y′Y'Y′ for which the same signature is also valid:

  1. Start with the verification equation: z⋅G=R+c⋅Yz \cdot G = R + c \cdot Yz⋅G=R+c⋅Y.
  2. Rearrange: Y′=c−1⋅(z⋅G−R)Y' = c^{-1} \cdot (z \cdot G - R)Y′=c−1⋅(z⋅G−R).
  3. The pair (R,z)(R, z)(R,z) now verifies under Y′Y'Y′ too, because R+c⋅Y′=R+c⋅c−1⋅(z⋅G−R)=z⋅GR + c \cdot Y' = R + c \cdot c^{-1} \cdot (z \cdot G - R) = z \cdot GR+c⋅Y′=R+c⋅c−1⋅(z⋅G−R)=z⋅G.

The attacker doesn't need to know the secret key for Y′Y'Y′ — they just need to find a point that makes the equation balance. This is called a key substitution attack (or "duplicate signature key selection").

Why does this matter in practice? Consider a multi-party protocol where you need to prove that a specific participant signed a message. Without YYY in the hash, an adversary could take a legitimate signature from Alice and reuse it to frame Bob — or vice versa. In threshold signing like FROST, this is especially dangerous: the protocol relies on verifying that each participant produced their own valid signature share under their own verification key YpY_pYp​.

Including YYY in the hash ties the challenge (and therefore the entire signature) to a specific public key. The same (R,z)(R, z)(R,z) pair produces a different ccc for a different YYY, so it won't verify under any other key.

This is analyzed in the multi-user security setting by Menezes & Smart (2004). Ed25519 and BIP-340 (Bitcoin's Schnorr scheme) both include YYY in the hash for this reason.

Why the nonce is the most critical detail

Look at the response equation again: z=k+s⋅cz = k + s \cdot cz=k+s⋅c. Both zzz (published in the signature) and ccc (computed from public data) are known to everyone. The only thing stopping an attacker from solving for the secret key sss is the nonce kkk:

s=z−kcs = \frac{z - k}{c}s=cz−k​

If the nonce leaks, the secret key is immediately exposed. If the same nonce kkk is reused for two different messages (producing two different challenges c1,c2c_1, c_2c1​,c2​ and responses z1,z2z_1, z_2z1​,z2​), an attacker can set up two equations and solve for sss:

z1=k+s⋅c1z_1 = k + s \cdot c_1z1​=k+s⋅c1​ z2=k+s⋅c2z_2 = k + s \cdot c_2z2​=k+s⋅c2​

Subtract: z1−z2=s⋅(c1−c2)z_1 - z_2 = s \cdot (c_1 - c_2)z1​−z2​=s⋅(c1​−c2​), so s=z1−z2c1−c2s = \frac{z_1 - z_2}{c_1 - c_2}s=c1​−c2​z1​−z2​​. Game over. This is why nonces must be truly random, used exactly once, and immediately deleted. This matters even more in FROST, where multiple parties each contribute nonces.

A concrete example with small numbers

In real systems these are 256-bit numbers, but the math is identical with small ones. Let's work modulo q=23q = 23q=23.

  • Secret key: s=7s = 7s=7
  • Public key: Y=7GY = 7GY=7G
  • Nonce: k=13k = 13k=13, so commitment: R=13GR = 13GR=13G
  • Suppose the hash gives us: c=H(R∥Y∥m)=5c = H(R \| Y \| m) = 5c=H(R∥Y∥m)=5
  • Response: z=k+s⋅c=13+7⋅5=48≡2(mod23)z = k + s \cdot c = 13 + 7 \cdot 5 = 48 \equiv 2 \pmod{23}z=k+s⋅c=13+7⋅5=48≡2(mod23)

Verification: Is z⋅G=R+c⋅Yz \cdot G = R + c \cdot Yz⋅G=R+c⋅Y?

  • Left side: 2G2G2G
  • Right side: 13G+5⋅7G=13G+35G=48G≡2G(mod23)13G + 5 \cdot 7G = 13G + 35G = 48G \equiv 2G \pmod{23}13G+5⋅7G=13G+35G=48G≡2G(mod23)

Both sides equal 2G2G2G. The signature is valid.

Aggregating nonce R

Now let's move toward multi-party signing. Suppose two signers want to jointly produce a signature. Each picks their own random nonce: signer 1 picks k1k_1k1​ and publishes R1=k1⋅GR_1 = k_1 \cdot GR1​=k1​⋅G, signer 2 picks k2k_2k2​ and publishes R2=k2⋅GR_2 = k_2 \cdot GR2​=k2​⋅G.

The simplest idea: just add them together.

R=R1+R2=(k1+k2)⋅GR = R_1 + R_2 = (k_1 + k_2) \cdot GR=R1​+R2​=(k1​+k2​)⋅G

The group's nonce is k1+k2k_1 + k_2k1​+k2​ and the group's commitment is R1+R2R_1 + R_2R1​+R2​. This is called additive nonce aggregation, and it almost works — except for a devastating attack.

Why naive aggregation is dangerous

Suppose signer 2 is malicious. The honest signer 1 publishes R1R_1R1​ first. The attacker waits, sees R1R_1R1​, and then computes:

R2=Rtarget−R1R_2 = R_{\text{target}} - R_1R2​=Rtarget​−R1​

for some RtargetR_{\text{target}}Rtarget​ they chose in advance. Now the aggregate is R=R1+R2=RtargetR = R_1 + R_2 = R_{\text{target}}R=R1​+R2​=Rtarget​ — the attacker has complete control over the group commitment.

Why is this bad? The challenge c=H(R∥Y∥m)c = H(R \| Y \| m)c=H(R∥Y∥m) depends on RRR. If the attacker controls RRR, they can precompute the challenge and craft their contribution to forge a signature. This is called a nonce manipulation attack.

The root cause: the attacker gets to see the honest party's commitment before choosing their own. They can "cancel out" the honest contribution and replace it with whatever they want.

The fix: binding factors

FROST solves this by adding a twist. Instead of each signer committing to one nonce value, they commit to two values, and these get combined using a binding factor — a hash-derived number that depends on everyone's commitments.

Each participant PpP_pPp​ publishes two commitments:

  • Dp=dp⋅GD_p = d_p \cdot GDp​=dp​⋅G (the "hiding" commitment)
  • Ep=ep⋅GE_p = e_p \cdot GEp​=ep​⋅G (the "binding" commitment)

After everyone has published, the binding factor for each participant is computed as:

ρp=H(Y∥all commitments∥m∥p)\rho_p = H\big(Y \| \text{all commitments} \| m \| p\big)ρp​=H(Y∥all commitments∥m∥p)

The group commitment is then:

R=∑p∈S(Dp+ρp⋅Ep)R = \sum_{p \in S} \left( D_p + \rho_p \cdot E_p \right)R=p∈S∑​(Dp​+ρp​⋅Ep​)

The key insight: ρp\rho_pρp​ is a hash of all commitments, so it can only be computed after everyone has already published (Dp,Ep)(D_p, E_p)(Dp​,Ep​). If any signer changes their commitment, every binding factor changes, invalidating any precomputed attack. The attacker can no longer manipulate RRR because they'd need to predict the hash output before it's computable.

Why two commitments instead of one?

If each signer only published one commitment RpR_pRp​ and we mixed it with a binding factor as ρp⋅Rp\rho_p \cdot R_pρp​⋅Rp​, the attacker could still manipulate things — they have one unknown (RpR_pRp​) but also one equation to satisfy. Two independent commitments (Dp,Ep)(D_p, E_p)(Dp​,Ep​) combined as Dp+ρp⋅EpD_p + \rho_p \cdot E_pDp​+ρp​⋅Ep​ give the binding factor something to "entangle" with. The attacker would need to predict ρp\rho_pρp​ before choosing EpE_pEp​, but ρp\rho_pρp​ depends on EpE_pEp​ — a chicken-and-egg problem that defeats the attack.

Why does FROST need per-participant binding factors?

In MuSig2 (an nnn-of-nnn multisignature scheme where all signers must participate), a single binding factor bbb — the same for everyone — is sufficient. That's because the signing set is fixed: the adversary can't choose which honest parties to include.

FROST is a threshold scheme (ttt-of-nnn): only ttt signers are needed. An adversary controlling t−1t-1t−1 parties can start multiple parallel signing sessions, each time pairing their corrupt parties with a different honest signer. If the binding factor were the same for all participants, the adversary could correlate honest signers' nonces across sessions and forge signatures (this is called Wagner's generalized birthday attack).

FROST defeats this by including the participant's identifier ppp in the binding factor hash. Different participants get different ρp\rho_pρp​ values, so the adversary can't correlate nonce contributions across sessions.

Aggregating partial signatures

Now we know how to safely combine nonces. The next question: how do we combine each signer's contribution into a single valid Schnorr signature?

Each signer produces a signature share (also called a partial signature) — a number zpz_pzp​ computed from their own secrets and nonces. The design ensures that when you add up all the shares, you get a valid Schnorr response.

The signature share equation

Recall that a standard Schnorr response is z=k+s⋅cz = k + s \cdot cz=k+s⋅c. In FROST, each participant PpP_pPp​ computes their share as:

zp=dp+ρp⋅ep+λp⋅sp⋅cz_p = d_p + \rho_p \cdot e_p + \lambda_p \cdot s_p \cdot czp​=dp​+ρp​⋅ep​+λp​⋅sp​⋅c

Let's break down each term:

  • dp+ρp⋅epd_p + \rho_p \cdot e_pdp​+ρp​⋅ep​ — this is PpP_pPp​'s contribution to the aggregate nonce. It matches their commitments Dp+ρp⋅EpD_p + \rho_p \cdot E_pDp​+ρp​⋅Ep​ that went into computing RRR.
  • λp\lambda_pλp​ — the Lagrange coefficient, a weight that depends on which set of signers is participating. We'll explain this in detail in the next sections. For now, just know that these weights ensure the secret shares add up correctly.
  • sps_psp​ — participant PpP_pPp​'s secret share (their piece of the group secret key).
  • c=H(R∥Y∥m)c = H(R \| Y \| m)c=H(R∥Y∥m) — the challenge, same as in regular Schnorr.

Why the sum of shares equals a valid signature

When we add up all ttt signature shares:

z=∑p∈Szp=∑p∈S(dp+ρp⋅ep)⏟adds up to k+  c⋅∑p∈Sλp⋅sp⏟adds up to sz = \sum_{p \in S} z_p = \underbrace{\sum_{p \in S} (d_p + \rho_p \cdot e_p)}_{\text{adds up to } k} + \; c \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{p \in S} \lambda_p \cdot s_p}_{\text{adds up to } s}z=p∈S∑​zp​=adds up to kp∈S∑​(dp​+ρp​⋅ep​)​​+c⋅adds up to sp∈S∑​λp​⋅sp​​​

Two things happen:

  1. The nonce parts sum to kkk — the discrete log of the group commitment RRR. This is by construction: RRR was defined as the sum of (Dp+ρp⋅Ep)(D_p + \rho_p \cdot E_p)(Dp​+ρp​⋅Ep​), so the corresponding scalars sum to kkk.

  2. The weighted secret shares sum to sss — the group secret key. This is where Lagrange interpolation (covered below) does its magic: the λp\lambda_pλp​ weights are chosen so that ∑λp⋅sp=s\sum \lambda_p \cdot s_p = s∑λp​⋅sp​=s.

Together: z=k+s⋅cz = k + s \cdot cz=k+s⋅c, which is exactly a valid Schnorr response. The verifier checks z⋅G=?R+c⋅Yz \cdot G \stackrel{?}{=} R + c \cdot Yz⋅G=?R+c⋅Y and it passes — nobody needs to know that zzz was computed by multiple parties.

Checking individual shares (identifiable abort)

Before adding the shares up, the Coordinator can verify each one individually:

zp⋅G=?Dp+ρp⋅Ep+(λp⋅c)⋅Ypz_p \cdot G \stackrel{?}{=} D_p + \rho_p \cdot E_p + (\lambda_p \cdot c) \cdot Y_pzp​⋅G=?Dp​+ρp​⋅Ep​+(λp​⋅c)⋅Yp​

where Yp=sp⋅GY_p = s_p \cdot GYp​=sp​⋅G is PpP_pPp​'s public verification share — a publicly known point that corresponds to their secret share. This check uses only public values (no secrets revealed). If a participant sends a bad share, the Coordinator can identify them and abort. This is why FROST has identifiable abort — you can always tell who cheated.

A concrete example

Let's trace through partial signature aggregation with numbers. We'll use the Shamir shares from the next section (feel free to jump ahead and come back):

  • t=2t = 2t=2, n=3n = 3n=3, signing set S={1,2}S = \{1, 2\}S={1,2}
  • Group secret: s=16s = 16s=16, challenge: c=5c = 5c=5
  • Secret shares: s1=22s_1 = 22s1​=22, s2=28s_2 = 28s2​=28
  • Lagrange coefficients for S={1,2}S = \{1, 2\}S={1,2}: λ1=2\lambda_1 = 2λ1​=2, λ2=−1\lambda_2 = -1λ2​=−1
  • Nonces: d1=4d_1 = 4d1​=4, e1=3e_1 = 3e1​=3, d2=6d_2 = 6d2​=6, e2=2e_2 = 2e2​=2
  • Binding factors: ρ1=7\rho_1 = 7ρ1​=7, ρ2=11\rho_2 = 11ρ2​=11

Each participant computes their share by plugging into zp=dp+ρp⋅ep+λp⋅sp⋅cz_p = d_p + \rho_p \cdot e_p + \lambda_p \cdot s_p \cdot czp​=dp​+ρp​⋅ep​+λp​⋅sp​⋅c:

z1=4+7⋅3+2⋅22⋅5=4+21+220=245z_1 = 4 + 7 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 22 \cdot 5 = 4 + 21 + 220 = 245z1​=4+7⋅3+2⋅22⋅5=4+21+220=245 z2=6+11⋅2+(−1)⋅28⋅5=6+22−140=−112z_2 = 6 + 11 \cdot 2 + (-1) \cdot 28 \cdot 5 = 6 + 22 - 140 = -112z2​=6+11⋅2+(−1)⋅28⋅5=6+22−140=−112

The Coordinator sums them:

z=z1+z2=245+(−112)=133z = z_1 + z_2 = 245 + (-112) = 133z=z1​+z2​=245+(−112)=133

Let's verify this equals k+s⋅ck + s \cdot ck+s⋅c. The aggregate nonce is k=(4+7⋅3)+(6+11⋅2)=25+28=53k = (4 + 7 \cdot 3) + (6 + 11 \cdot 2) = 25 + 28 = 53k=(4+7⋅3)+(6+11⋅2)=25+28=53. The reconstructed secret is ∑λp⋅sp=2⋅22+(−1)⋅28=16=s\sum \lambda_p \cdot s_p = 2 \cdot 22 + (-1) \cdot 28 = 16 = s∑λp​⋅sp​=2⋅22+(−1)⋅28=16=s. So:

k+s⋅c=53+16⋅5=133✓k + s \cdot c = 53 + 16 \cdot 5 = 133 \quad \checkmarkk+s⋅c=53+16⋅5=133✓

It works. The sum of partial signatures is a valid Schnorr response.

Shamir Secret Sharing

We've been using "secret shares" sps_psp​ and "Lagrange coefficients" λp\lambda_pλp​ without fully explaining where they come from. Let's fix that.

The core problem: we need to split the secret key sss among nnn participants so that:

  • Any ttt participants can reconstruct sss (by combining their shares)
  • Any t−1t - 1t−1 participants learn absolutely nothing about sss

This is Shamir's Secret Sharing (1979), and it's built on a beautifully simple idea from algebra.

The key insight: polynomials and points

A straight line (y=ax+by = ax + by=ax+b) is uniquely determined by 2 points. A parabola (y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c) is uniquely determined by 3 points. In general, a polynomial of degree ddd is uniquely determined by d+1d + 1d+1 points.

Shamir's trick: to create a (t,n)(t, n)(t,n) sharing scheme, embed the secret as the constant term of a random polynomial of degree t−1t - 1t−1. Then distribute nnn points on that polynomial. Any ttt points determine the polynomial (and thus the secret), but t−1t - 1t−1 points leave the secret completely undetermined.

How it works

The dealer (the entity splitting the secret) picks a random polynomial of degree t−1t - 1t−1:

f(x)=s+a1x+a2x2+⋯+at−1xt−1f(x) = s + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_{t-1} x^{t-1}f(x)=s+a1​x+a2​x2+⋯+at−1​xt−1

The constant term is the secret: f(0)=sf(0) = sf(0)=s. The other coefficients a1,…,at−1a_1, \dots, a_{t-1}a1​,…,at−1​ are random. Each participant PpP_pPp​ receives the share sp=f(p)s_p = f(p)sp​=f(p) — the polynomial evaluated at their index.

Concrete example

Let's set up a (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3) scheme — any 2 of 3 participants can reconstruct, 1 participant alone learns nothing. Our secret is s=16s = 16s=16.

Since t=2t = 2t=2, we need a degree-1 polynomial (a line): f(x)=16+6xf(x) = 16 + 6xf(x)=16+6x (the coefficient 666 is chosen randomly).

Compute the shares by evaluating fff at each participant's index:

  • P1P_1P1​ gets s1=f(1)=16+6=22s_1 = f(1) = 16 + 6 = 22s1​=f(1)=16+6=22
  • P2P_2P2​ gets s2=f(2)=16+12=28s_2 = f(2) = 16 + 12 = 28s2​=f(2)=16+12=28
  • P3P_3P3​ gets s3=f(3)=16+18=34s_3 = f(3) = 16 + 18 = 34s3​=f(3)=16+18=34

Why is this secure? The shares are points on a line. Two points determine a line, so any 2 shares let you find fff and compute f(0)=16=sf(0) = 16 = sf(0)=16=s. But a single point, say (1,22)(1, 22)(1,22), tells you nothing: for any possible secret s′s's′, there's a line through (1,22)(1, 22)(1,22) with yyy-intercept s′s's′. One share is consistent with every possible secret.

The dealer problem: who picks the polynomial?

In the basic scheme, a single dealer knows the secret, creates the polynomial, and distributes shares. But in a decentralized system (like a blockchain bridge), there shouldn't be anyone who ever knows the full secret. If the dealer is compromised during setup, the whole scheme fails.

The solution is Distributed Key Generation (DKG) — the participants collectively generate a shared secret where nobody, not even during setup, ever knows the full key.

Pedersen DKG: generating a shared secret with no trusted dealer

The idea is elegant: instead of one dealer picking one polynomial, every participant picks their own random polynomial and shares pieces of it with everyone else. The group secret emerges as the sum of everyone's individual secrets, but no one ever computes that sum.

Here's how it works. Each of the nnn participants PjP_jPj​ independently:

  1. Picks a random polynomial fj(x)f_j(x)fj​(x) of degree t−1t - 1t−1. The constant term aj,0a_{j,0}aj,0​ is PjP_jPj​'s private contribution to the group secret.

  2. Publishes commitments to their polynomial's coefficients: Cj,k=aj,k⋅GC_{j,k} = a_{j,k} \cdot GCj,k​=aj,k​⋅G for each coefficient kkk. These are elliptic curve points — they "commit" PjP_jPj​ to their polynomial without revealing the actual coefficients (the discrete log problem protects them).

  3. Privately sends fj(p)f_j(p)fj​(p) to each participant PpP_pPp​. This is the value of PjP_jPj​'s polynomial evaluated at PpP_pPp​'s index.

  4. Publishes a proof that they know their secret aj,0a_{j,0}aj,0​ (a Schnorr proof of knowledge). This prevents a "rogue-key attack" where a malicious participant claims a carefully crafted public key to manipulate the group key.

After everyone has done this, each participant PpP_pPp​ adds up all the values they received:

sp=∑j=1nfj(p)s_p = \sum_{j=1}^{n} f_j(p)sp​=j=1∑n​fj​(p)

This is PpP_pPp​'s combined secret share. It's a sum of contributions from every participant.

The group secret (which nobody ever computes explicitly!) is:

s=∑j=1nfj(0)=∑j=1naj,0s = \sum_{j=1}^{n} f_j(0) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{j,0}s=j=1∑n​fj​(0)=j=1∑n​aj,0​

The group public key is computable from the published commitments:

Y=s⋅G=∑j=1nCj,0Y = s \cdot G = \sum_{j=1}^{n} C_{j,0}Y=s⋅G=j=1∑n​Cj,0​

Why does this work as Shamir sharing? The combined shares sps_psp​ are points on a "virtual" polynomial F(x)=∑j=1nfj(x)F(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} f_j(x)F(x)=∑j=1n​fj​(x). This polynomial has degree t−1t - 1t−1 (sum of degree-(t−1)(t-1)(t−1) polynomials) and F(0)=sF(0) = sF(0)=s. So the combined shares are exactly Shamir shares of the group secret sss — even though nobody ever chose FFF deliberately.

Concrete DKG example

n=3n = 3n=3, t=2t = 2t=2. Each participant independently picks a degree-1 (line) polynomial:

  • P1P_1P1​ picks: f1(x)=7+3xf_1(x) = 7 + 3xf1​(x)=7+3x (their secret contribution is 777)
  • P2P_2P2​ picks: f2(x)=5+2xf_2(x) = 5 + 2xf2​(x)=5+2x (their secret contribution is 555)
  • P3P_3P3​ picks: f3(x)=4+xf_3(x) = 4 + xf3​(x)=4+x (their secret contribution is 444)

Now each participant evaluates their polynomial at everyone's index and sends the result privately:

Sender evaluates at →P₁ (p=1)P₂ (p=2)P₃ (p=3)
P₁: f₁(p)7 + 3 = 107 + 6 = 137 + 9 = 16
P₂: f₂(p)5 + 2 = 75 + 4 = 95 + 6 = 11
P₃: f₃(p)4 + 1 = 54 + 2 = 64 + 3 = 7

Each participant sums the column they received:

  • P1P_1P1​: s1=10+7+5=22s_1 = 10 + 7 + 5 = 22s1​=10+7+5=22
  • P2P_2P2​: s2=13+9+6=28s_2 = 13 + 9 + 6 = 28s2​=13+9+6=28
  • P3P_3P3​: s3=16+11+7=34s_3 = 16 + 11 + 7 = 34s3​=16+11+7=34

The virtual polynomial is: F(x)=(7+5+4)+(3+2+1)x=16+6xF(x) = (7 + 5 + 4) + (3 + 2 + 1)x = 16 + 6xF(x)=(7+5+4)+(3+2+1)x=16+6x

The group secret is: s=F(0)=16s = F(0) = 16s=F(0)=16 — but nobody computed this! P1P_1P1​ only knows 777 (their own contribution), P2P_2P2​ only knows 555, P3P_3P3​ only knows 444.

The group public key: Y=16G=7G+5G+4GY = 16G = 7G + 5G + 4GY=16G=7G+5G+4G — anyone can compute this from the published commitments.

Feldman VSS: verifying that shares are correct

There's a trust problem: when PjP_jPj​ sends fj(p)f_j(p)fj​(p) to PpP_pPp​, how does PpP_pPp​ know the value is correct? PjP_jPj​ could send garbage or strategically wrong values. We need a way to verify shares without revealing the polynomial.

This is where the published commitments Cj,k=aj,k⋅GC_{j,k} = a_{j,k} \cdot GCj,k​=aj,k​⋅G become essential. Participant PpP_pPp​ can check:

fj(p)⋅G=?∑k=0t−1pk⋅Cj,kf_j(p) \cdot G \stackrel{?}{=} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} p^k \cdot C_{j,k}fj​(p)⋅G=?k=0∑t−1​pk⋅Cj,k​

Left side: multiply the generator by the share value (a single scalar-point multiplication).

Right side: evaluate the "committed polynomial" at ppp using the public commitments. This works because:

∑k=0t−1pk⋅Cj,k=∑k=0t−1pk⋅aj,k⋅G=(∑k=0t−1aj,k⋅pk)⋅G=fj(p)⋅G\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} p^k \cdot C_{j,k} = \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} p^k \cdot a_{j,k} \cdot G = \left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} a_{j,k} \cdot p^k\right) \cdot G = f_j(p) \cdot Gk=0∑t−1​pk⋅Cj,k​=k=0∑t−1​pk⋅aj,k​⋅G=(k=0∑t−1​aj,k​⋅pk)⋅G=fj​(p)⋅G

Both sides compute fj(p)⋅Gf_j(p) \cdot Gfj​(p)⋅G by different paths. The left side uses the secret share value. The right side uses only public commitments. If they match, the share is consistent with the published commitments. If they don't, PjP_jPj​ cheated and can be identified.

The beauty: the verification happens entirely "in the exponent" (on elliptic curve points). Nobody learns the polynomial coefficients — they only verify consistency.

Lagrange Interpolation

We now have ttt participants, each holding a share sp=F(p)s_p = F(p)sp​=F(p) — a point on a secret polynomial FFF of degree t−1t - 1t−1. We need to recover F(0)=sF(0) = sF(0)=s (the group secret) without anyone actually reconstructing the polynomial.

Lagrange interpolation gives us a formula that computes F(0)F(0)F(0) directly from ttt points, as a weighted sum of the share values.

Building the intuition

Suppose you have 2 points on a line and want to find where it crosses the yyy-axis (i.e., the value at x=0x = 0x=0). You could find the slope, write the line equation, and plug in x=0x = 0x=0. Lagrange interpolation is a general formula that does this for polynomials of any degree — and it gives the answer as a weighted sum of the known yyy-values.

The formula

Given a signing set SSS of ttt participants, each with share sp=F(p)s_p = F(p)sp​=F(p), the secret is:

s=F(0)=∑p∈Sλp⋅sps = F(0) = \sum_{p \in S} \lambda_p \cdot s_ps=F(0)=p∈S∑​λp​⋅sp​

where the Lagrange coefficient for participant PpP_pPp​ is:

λp=∏q∈Sq≠pqq−p\lambda_p = \prod_{\substack{q \in S \\ q \neq p}} \frac{q}{q - p}λp​=q∈Sq=p​∏​q−pq​

This formula looks intimidating, but it's just a product of fractions involving the participant indices. Let's see it in action.

Where does this formula come from?

The Lagrange interpolation formula for a polynomial g(x)g(x)g(x) passing through points (p,g(p))(p, g(p))(p,g(p)) for p∈Sp \in Sp∈S is:

g(x)=∑p∈Sg(p)⋅∏q∈Sq≠px−qp−q⏟Lp(x)g(x) = \sum_{p \in S} g(p) \cdot \underbrace{\prod_{\substack{q \in S \\ q \neq p}} \frac{x - q}{p - q}}_{L_p(x)}g(x)=p∈S∑​g(p)⋅Lp​(x)q∈Sq=p​∏​p−qx−q​​​

Each Lp(x)L_p(x)Lp​(x) is called a Lagrange basis polynomial. It has a key property: Lp(p)=1L_p(p) = 1Lp​(p)=1 and Lp(q)=0L_p(q) = 0Lp​(q)=0 for every other q∈Sq \in Sq∈S. So each basis polynomial "selects" exactly one data point.

We only need g(0)g(0)g(0), so we plug in x=0x = 0x=0:

g(0)=∑p∈Sg(p)⋅∏q∈Sq≠p0−qp−q=∑p∈Sg(p)⋅∏q∈Sq≠pqq−pg(0) = \sum_{p \in S} g(p) \cdot \prod_{\substack{q \in S \\ q \neq p}} \frac{0 - q}{p - q} = \sum_{p \in S} g(p) \cdot \prod_{\substack{q \in S \\ q \neq p}} \frac{q}{q - p}g(0)=p∈S∑​g(p)⋅q∈Sq=p​∏​p−q0−q​=p∈S∑​g(p)⋅q∈Sq=p​∏​q−pq​

The last step is the sign flip: 0−qp−q=−qp−q=qq−p\frac{0-q}{p-q} = \frac{-q}{p-q} = \frac{q}{q-p}p−q0−q​=p−q−q​=q−pq​.

Concrete examples

Using our shares: s1=22s_1 = 22s1​=22, s2=28s_2 = 28s2​=28, s3=34s_3 = 34s3​=34. The secret is s=16s = 16s=16.

With participants S={1,2}S = \{1, 2\}S={1,2}:

λ1=22−1=2,λ2=11−2=−1\lambda_1 = \frac{2}{2 - 1} = 2, \qquad \lambda_2 = \frac{1}{1 - 2} = -1λ1​=2−12​=2,λ2​=1−21​=−1 s=2⋅22+(−1)⋅28=44−28=16✓s = 2 \cdot 22 + (-1) \cdot 28 = 44 - 28 = 16 \quad \checkmarks=2⋅22+(−1)⋅28=44−28=16✓

With participants S={2,3}S = \{2, 3\}S={2,3}:

λ2=33−2=3,λ3=22−3=−2\lambda_2 = \frac{3}{3 - 2} = 3, \qquad \lambda_3 = \frac{2}{2 - 3} = -2λ2​=3−23​=3,λ3​=2−32​=−2 s=3⋅28+(−2)⋅34=84−68=16✓s = 3 \cdot 28 + (-2) \cdot 34 = 84 - 68 = 16 \quad \checkmarks=3⋅28+(−2)⋅34=84−68=16✓

With participants S={1,3}S = \{1, 3\}S={1,3}:

λ1=33−1=32,λ3=11−3=−12\lambda_1 = \frac{3}{3 - 1} = \frac{3}{2}, \qquad \lambda_3 = \frac{1}{1 - 3} = -\frac{1}{2}λ1​=3−13​=23​,λ3​=1−31​=−21​ s=32⋅22+(−12)⋅34=33−17=16✓s = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 22 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \cdot 34 = 33 - 17 = 16 \quad \checkmarks=23​⋅22+(−21​)⋅34=33−17=16✓

Every pair recovers the same secret. The Lagrange coefficients are different for different sets of participants, but the weighted sum always yields s=16s = 16s=16. This is the mathematical guarantee of Shamir's scheme.

The critical property for FROST

Notice that Lagrange interpolation is a linear operation — the secret is a weighted sum of the shares:

∑p∈Sλp⋅sp=s\sum_{p \in S} \lambda_p \cdot s_p = sp∈S∑​λp​⋅sp​=s

This linearity is what makes threshold Schnorr signatures possible. Each participant multiplies their share sps_psp​ by λp⋅c\lambda_p \cdot cλp​⋅c and contributes that to the signature. Nobody reconstructs sss — they each contribute their weighted piece, and the sum magically equals s⋅cs \cdot cs⋅c.

In curve-point terms:

∑p∈Sλp⋅(sp⋅G)=s⋅G=Y\sum_{p \in S} \lambda_p \cdot (s_p \cdot G) = s \cdot G = Yp∈S∑​λp​⋅(sp​⋅G)=s⋅G=Y

The Lagrange recombination works both in the scalar world (secret numbers) and in the point world (public keys). This "homomorphic" property — the ability to do the computation "in the exponent" — is the mathematical backbone of FROST.

FROST Protocol

We've built all the pieces. Now let's put them together into the actual FROST protocol: a two-round scheme where ttt of nnn participants cooperatively produce a standard Schnorr signature.

Setup: Distributed Key Generation (done once)

Before any signing can happen, the participants run the Pedersen DKG described above. Afterward, each participant PpP_pPp​ holds:

  • Their secret share sps_psp​ (private — never revealed)
  • The group public key Y=s⋅GY = s \cdot GY=s⋅G (public — this is the address that will verify signatures)
  • Public verification shares Yp=sp⋅GY_p = s_p \cdot GYp​=sp​⋅G for all participants (public — used to verify individual signature shares)

Roles

  • Participants P1,…,PnP_1, \dots, P_nP1​,…,Pn​: hold secret shares, produce signature shares. At least ttt must be online for any given signing session.
  • Coordinator (also called Signature Aggregator): orchestrates the protocol, collects commitments and shares, produces the final signature. The Coordinator is semi-trusted — they cannot learn the secret key or forge signatures (even a corrupt Coordinator can't sign without ttt honest participants). However, a corrupt Coordinator can refuse to produce the signature (denial of service) or falsely blame a participant for sending a bad share.

Round 1: Commitment

Each participant PpP_pPp​ in the signing set SSS (where ∣S∣≥t|S| \geq t∣S∣≥t):

  1. Generates two random nonces: dpd_pdp​ and epe_pep​ (random scalars). These are generated as H(random_bytes(32)∥skp)H(\text{random\_bytes}(32) \| sk_p)H(random_bytes(32)∥skp​) — mixing randomness with the secret key as a hedge against a faulty random number generator.

  2. Computes commitments: Dp=dp⋅GD_p = d_p \cdot GDp​=dp​⋅G and Ep=ep⋅GE_p = e_p \cdot GEp​=ep​⋅G.

  3. Sends (Dp,Ep)(D_p, E_p)(Dp​,Ep​) to the Coordinator.

After Round 1, the Coordinator has everyone's commitments, but nobody knows anyone else's nonce values (dpd_pdp​, epe_pep​), only the corresponding curve points.

Critical safety rule: each (dp,ep)(d_p, e_p)(dp​,ep​) pair must be used in exactly one signing session. If a signing session is aborted, the nonces must be discarded and fresh ones generated for any retry. Reusing nonces across sessions can leak the secret key.

Round 2: Signature Share

The Coordinator broadcasts the message mmm to sign and the full list of all commitments (Dp,Ep)(D_p, E_p)(Dp​,Ep​) for every p∈Sp \in Sp∈S.

Each participant PpP_pPp​ then independently computes:

Step 1. Binding factors. Compute the binding factor for each participant:

ρp=H1(Y∥H4(m)∥H5(all commitments)∥p)\rho_p = H_1\big(Y \| H_4(m) \| H_5(\text{all commitments}) \| p\big)ρp​=H1​(Y∥H4​(m)∥H5​(all commitments)∥p)

The subscripts H1,H4,H5H_1, H_4, H_5H1​,H4​,H5​ denote domain-separated hash functions — they use different prefixes so that a hash computed for one purpose can't be confused with a hash for a different purpose. This is a standard defensive practice in cryptographic protocols.

Every participant computes the same ρp\rho_pρp​ values because they all have the same inputs (all commitments were broadcast).

Step 2. Group commitment. Compute the aggregate nonce point:

R=∑p∈S(Dp+ρp⋅Ep)R = \sum_{p \in S} \left(D_p + \rho_p \cdot E_p\right)R=p∈S∑​(Dp​+ρp​⋅Ep​)

Again, every participant gets the same RRR.

Step 3. Challenge. Compute the Schnorr challenge:

c=H2(R∥Y∥m)c = H_2(R \| Y \| m)c=H2​(R∥Y∥m)

Step 4. Lagrange coefficient. Compute λp\lambda_pλp​ for participant PpP_pPp​ given the signing set SSS.

Step 5. Signature share. Compute and send:

zp=dp+ρp⋅ep+λp⋅sp⋅cz_p = d_p + \rho_p \cdot e_p + \lambda_p \cdot s_p \cdot czp​=dp​+ρp​⋅ep​+λp​⋅sp​⋅c

This is the moment where the participant uses their secret share sps_psp​. After computing zpz_pzp​, they delete dpd_pdp​ and epe_pep​ immediately.

Step 6. Send zpz_pzp​ to the Coordinator.

Aggregation

The Coordinator now has all ttt signature shares zpz_pzp​. They:

  1. (Optional but recommended) Verify each share:
zp⋅G=?Dp+ρp⋅Ep+(λp⋅c)⋅Ypz_p \cdot G \stackrel{?}{=} D_p + \rho_p \cdot E_p + (\lambda_p \cdot c) \cdot Y_pzp​⋅G=?Dp​+ρp​⋅Ep​+(λp​⋅c)⋅Yp​

If any share fails, the Coordinator identifies the misbehaving participant and aborts.

  1. Aggregate:
z=∑p∈Szpz = \sum_{p \in S} z_pz=p∈S∑​zp​
  1. Output the signature: σ=(R,z)\sigma = (R, z)σ=(R,z)

This signature passes standard Schnorr verification: z⋅G=?R+c⋅Yz \cdot G \stackrel{?}{=} R + c \cdot Yz⋅G=?R+c⋅Y.

Why it's correct

Let's trace through the math one more time:

z=∑p∈Szp=∑p∈S(dp+ρp⋅ep)+c⋅∑p∈Sλp⋅spz = \sum_{p \in S} z_p = \sum_{p \in S} (d_p + \rho_p \cdot e_p) + c \cdot \sum_{p \in S} \lambda_p \cdot s_pz=p∈S∑​zp​=p∈S∑​(dp​+ρp​⋅ep​)+c⋅p∈S∑​λp​⋅sp​

The nonce terms sum to kkk (the discrete log of RRR):

∑p∈S(dp+ρp⋅ep)⋅G=∑p∈S(Dp+ρp⋅Ep)=R⇒sum=k\sum_{p \in S} (d_p + \rho_p \cdot e_p) \cdot G = \sum_{p \in S} (D_p + \rho_p \cdot E_p) = R \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{sum} = kp∈S∑​(dp​+ρp​⋅ep​)⋅G=p∈S∑​(Dp​+ρp​⋅Ep​)=R⇒sum=k

The secret share terms recover sss by Lagrange interpolation:

∑p∈Sλp⋅sp=s\sum_{p \in S} \lambda_p \cdot s_p = sp∈S∑​λp​⋅sp​=s

Therefore z=k+c⋅sz = k + c \cdot sz=k+c⋅s, and z⋅G=k⋅G+c⋅s⋅G=R+c⋅Yz \cdot G = k \cdot G + c \cdot s \cdot G = R + c \cdot Yz⋅G=k⋅G+c⋅s⋅G=R+c⋅Y. Valid Schnorr.

Complete worked example

Let's trace the entire FROST protocol end-to-end with concrete numbers. We'll work modulo q=97q = 97q=97 to keep the arithmetic manageable.

DKG (already done). Virtual polynomial F(x)=16+6x(mod97)F(x) = 16 + 6x \pmod{97}F(x)=16+6x(mod97).

  • Secret shares: s1=22s_1 = 22s1​=22, s2=28s_2 = 28s2​=28, s3=34s_3 = 34s3​=34
  • Group secret: s=16s = 16s=16 (nobody knows this)
  • Group public key: Y=16GY = 16GY=16G

Signing set: S={1,2}S = \{1, 2\}S={1,2} (participants P1P_1P1​ and P2P_2P2​ will sign)

Lagrange coefficients for S={1,2}S = \{1, 2\}S={1,2}:

λ1=22−1=2,λ2=11−2=−1≡96(mod97)\lambda_1 = \frac{2}{2 - 1} = 2, \qquad \lambda_2 = \frac{1}{1 - 2} = -1 \equiv 96 \pmod{97}λ1​=2−12​=2,λ2​=1−21​=−1≡96(mod97)

(In modular arithmetic, −1≡96(mod97)-1 \equiv 96 \pmod{97}−1≡96(mod97) because 96+1=97≡096 + 1 = 97 \equiv 096+1=97≡0.)

Round 1 — Each participant picks nonces and publishes commitments:

  • P1P_1P1​: d1=9d_1 = 9d1​=9, e1=14e_1 = 14e1​=14. Publishes D1=9GD_1 = 9GD1​=9G, E1=14GE_1 = 14GE1​=14G.
  • P2P_2P2​: d2=5d_2 = 5d2​=5, e2=11e_2 = 11e2​=11. Publishes D2=5GD_2 = 5GD2​=5G, E2=11GE_2 = 11GE2​=11G.

Round 2 — Compute everything and sign:

Binding factors (from hash — we'll suppose): ρ1=3\rho_1 = 3ρ1​=3, ρ2=7\rho_2 = 7ρ2​=7.

Group commitment:

R=(D1+3⋅E1)+(D2+7⋅E2)=(9+42)G+(5+77)G=51G+82G=133G≡36G(mod97)R = (D_1 + 3 \cdot E_1) + (D_2 + 7 \cdot E_2) = (9 + 42)G + (5 + 77)G = 51G + 82G = 133G \equiv 36G \pmod{97}R=(D1​+3⋅E1​)+(D2​+7⋅E2​)=(9+42)G+(5+77)G=51G+82G=133G≡36G(mod97)

So R=36GR = 36GR=36G, meaning the aggregate nonce is k=36k = 36k=36.

Challenge (from hash — we'll suppose): c=10c = 10c=10.

Signature shares:

P1P_1P1​:

z1=9+3⋅14+2⋅22⋅10=9+42+440=491≡491mod  97z_1 = 9 + 3 \cdot 14 + 2 \cdot 22 \cdot 10 = 9 + 42 + 440 = 491 \equiv 491 \mod 97z1​=9+3⋅14+2⋅22⋅10=9+42+440=491≡491mod97

491=5⋅97+6491 = 5 \cdot 97 + 6491=5⋅97+6, so z1=6z_1 = 6z1​=6.

P2P_2P2​:

z2=5+7⋅11+96⋅28⋅10=5+77+26880=26962≡26962mod  97z_2 = 5 + 7 \cdot 11 + 96 \cdot 28 \cdot 10 = 5 + 77 + 26880 = 26962 \equiv 26962 \mod 97z2​=5+7⋅11+96⋅28⋅10=5+77+26880=26962≡26962mod97

26962=277⋅97+9326962 = 277 \cdot 97 + 9326962=277⋅97+93, so z2=93z_2 = 93z2​=93.

Aggregation:

z=z1+z2=6+93=99≡2(mod97)z = z_1 + z_2 = 6 + 93 = 99 \equiv 2 \pmod{97}z=z1​+z2​=6+93=99≡2(mod97)

Verification — does this match a standard Schnorr signature?

k+s⋅c=36+16⋅10=196≡2(mod97)✓k + s \cdot c = 36 + 16 \cdot 10 = 196 \equiv 2 \pmod{97} \quad \checkmarkk+s⋅c=36+16⋅10=196≡2(mod97)✓ z⋅G=2G=?R+c⋅Y=36G+10⋅16G=36G+160G=196G≡2G(mod97)✓z \cdot G = 2G \stackrel{?}{=} R + c \cdot Y = 36G + 10 \cdot 16G = 36G + 160G = 196G \equiv 2G \pmod{97} \quad \checkmarkz⋅G=2G=?R+c⋅Y=36G+10⋅16G=36G+160G=196G≡2G(mod97)✓

The final signature is (R,z)=(36G,2)(R, z) = (36G, 2)(R,z)=(36G,2) — a perfectly valid Schnorr signature under the group public key Y=16GY = 16GY=16G. A verifier sees a normal-looking single-signer Schnorr signature. They have no way to know it was produced by two participants collaborating through FROST.

Summary of FROST properties

FROST produces a standard Schnorr signature — the output is indistinguishable from one created by a single signer. The protocol completes in 2 rounds (or just 1 if nonces are preprocessed). Any ttt of nnn participants can sign; the rest can be offline. Multiple signing sessions can run concurrently without compromising security.

If a participant misbehaves, the protocol provides identifiable abort — the cheater is detected, though a new session must be started without them. FROST is EUF-CMA secure under the One-More Discrete Log assumption: an adversary controlling up to t−1t-1t−1 participants cannot forge signatures.

The protocol is standardized in RFC 9591 (June 2024), with ciphersuites for Ed25519, Ed448, P-256, and secp256k1.
